author: NEIL JOHNSON
title: Janesville School District details coming school year for flood-displaced Washington Elementary students - NewsBreak
text:
By NEIL JOHNSON ,
14 hours ago
JANESVILLE — Janesville parents whose students would attend Washington Elementary School this coming school year learned new details of how the year will look as Washington remains closed after massive flooding in April.
District Superintendent Mark Holzman told parents the district has the summer to reconfigure space at Madison and Adams elementary schools — the two schools where Washington students were sent after the April 17 floods closed Washington. The game plan now is to configure the two buildings so Adams and Madison can absorb all the Washington class sections that will migrate to the schools for a full year in 2026-2027.
The result: Classroom sizes likely won’t balloon at either school because of the change, despite space being “tight” as it was more than a decade ago, when the district had about 1,000 more students enrolled than now.
Holzman said each student will get to eat lunch in the cafeteria, they’ll have dedicated art, music and physical education time, and they’ll all have access to their own locker.
“There will be no piling,” Holzman told about 75 parents, some who’d brought their children, to a special outreach meeting the district held for Washington school parents Wednesday night at Parker High School.
Holzman explained the district aims to use a survey that’s been sent to Washington school parents to learn their preferences on enrollment at Madison or Adams school, depending on whether a family has one or more children who would have attended Washington.
He said when the parent survey ends June 26, the district will use the results to help set teacher assignments and classroom rosters at both schools, and balance class sizes so “some classes don’t have 28 students and others have 16,” Holzman told parents.
The parent survey will also help the district and Van Galder bus set up neighborhood busing routes to allow students within the district’s Washington school attendance zone get bused to either Madison or Adams school.
What remains unclear is the longer-range picture for Washington Elementary — including whether it will reopen after what the district already knows will be at least a yearlong closure.
Right now, Holzman said, the district is running a diesel generator to keep air circulating the building, but its main power panel is down and will take about “40 weeks” of engineering and planning to get it back online. In preliminary discussions with the board this week, the district raised the specter that Washington may never reopen.
Holzman would not talk about Washington Elementary’s long-term future, telling parents that Wednesday’s outreach was about the immediate, upcoming school year — not long-range plans for what to do with Washington school.
“I don’t want to give you ‘This will happen,’ and then that happens,” Holzman told one parent who wondered if Washington might remain shuttered for good.
Holzman said discussions over the future of the school could take months, and any re-drawing of boundary lines for school enrollment would be a “big, big-picture” administrative discussion.
Washington has been closed since April 17, when torrential deluges totaling 8 or 10 inches in just hours filled North Pine Street, turning it into a river and dumping floodwater through the school’s doors.
Five feet of floodwater swamped the school’s basement, destroying major electrical and mechanical systems set there, and causing “significant impact” on parts of the school’s ground floor, including the school kitchen, cafeteria, and other classroom spaces.
Parents asked other questions, including when the district will decide on top leadership at Madison school.
The question came amid the district suddenly placing Madison Principal Stephanie Filter on paid administrative leave a few weeks ago. The district has not given details of why Filter is on leave.
Matt Peerenboom, Washington school’s principal, had been serving as interim principal at Madison school.
A parent asked if the district would have it decided who will be Madison’s principal before the Washington parents survey is due June 26.
“I mean, maybe, hopefully. I can’t guarantee you that, but we’re hopeful,” Holzman told the parent, saying the district was “working hard” on the issue.
The Gazette has filed an open records request with Janesville School District seeking records that would detail Filter’s leave at Madison school.

The result: Classroom sizes likely won’t balloon at either school because of the change, despite space being “tight” as it was more than a decade ago, when the district had about 1,000 more students enrolled than now.
